title: Quiz: subroutines
prompt: The procedure call standard: when a leaf routine can skip its frame, what 16-byte alignment actually demands, who prepares stack-passed arguments, and which registers survive a `bl`.

questions.question: A leaf subroutine does not call any other subroutines. Under what conditions can it avoid creating a stack frame?
options: If it does not modify any callee-saved registers and does not need stack storage for local data or spills.
If it uses only registers x0 through x7, regardless of what other storage it needs.
If it passes all arguments by reference.
If it returns a structure larger than 16 bytes.
questions.explanation: A leaf subroutine can skip the frame when it has nothing to preserve and nothing to store: no callee-saved registers written, no local data, no spills. Being a leaf is not enough on its own. The routine must also have no reason to touch the stack.
questions.hint: Ask what a stack frame is actually for. If the routine needs neither saved registers nor stack-based locals, does it need one?

questions.question: Which statement about stack alignment in AArch64 is correct?
options: Every subroutine must allocate at least 16 bytes for its stack frame.
sp must be 16-byte aligned at a public interface, but a subroutine does not necessarily need to allocate a stack frame.
Every stack frame must be exactly 16 bytes.
sp only needs to be aligned when the subroutine uses x29.
questions.explanation: AArch64 requires sp to be 16-byte aligned at a public interface, and any memory access through sp must use an aligned value or the program takes a bus error. That is a constraint on the value in sp, not a requirement that every routine allocate a frame: a leaf subroutine may need no frame at all.
questions.hint: Separate keeping sp correctly aligned from allocating space for a stack frame.

questions.question: A procedure is called with ten integer arguments. After the first eight arguments have been placed in x0 through x7, who is responsible for providing the stack memory used for the additional arguments?
options: The operating system.
The called subroutine (callee).
The calling code (caller).
The linker.
questions.explanation: The caller builds the argument area for anything passed in memory. The ninth and tenth values are written to the stack before the bl, so the callee reads them starting at the incoming sp.
questions.hint: The callee cannot read stack argument storage that nobody prepared before the call.

questions.question: What are x16 and x17 used for in the AArch64 procedure call standard?
options: They are callee-saved registers that must be preserved by every subroutine.
They are the indirect result location registers.
They are intra-procedure-call scratch registers, known as IP0 and IP1.
They are reserved for the frame pointer and the link register.
questions.explanation: x16 and x17 are the intra-procedure-call scratch registers IP0 and IP1. Linker-inserted veneers and other linkage code may clobber them across a call, so never expect a value in x16 or x17 to survive a bl.
questions.hint: The names carry 'IP' for intra-procedure. Think about temporary workspace used during a call.

questions.question: A calling function stores a value it still needs in x9, then executes bl. What must the calling function do?
options: Nothing. The called subroutine must preserve x9.
Preserve the value of x9 itself before the call and restore it afterward.
Move the value into x30, the link register.
Set x9 to zero before calling the subroutine.
questions.explanation: x9 is a caller-saved temporary, so the callee is free to overwrite it. If the caller needs the value after the call, the caller saves it first, typically into its own stack frame or into a callee-saved register such as x19.
questions.hint: The name 'caller-saved' names who is responsible for protecting the value.
